deities: Thimmamma (folk deity honoured by a small shrine beneath the tree)

history.period: Traditionally dated to 1434 CE (~550 years old; age from tradition, unverified)
history.summary: FLAG: Thimmamma Marrimanu is NOT a temple - it is a giant banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis) in Gutibayalu village, about 25 km from Kadiri in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, and is kept as a sacred-site record. Its canopy covers 19,107 square metres (4.72 acres) and it was recorded as the largest tree specimen in the world in the Guinness Book of World Records in 1989. Local legend holds that Thimmamma, daughter of a Settibalija couple (Sennakka Venkatappa and Mangamma, born AD 1394), committed sati on her husband Bala Veerayya's funeral pyre in 1434, and the tree sprouted from one of the pyre's poles. The tree is revered by Hindus, Buddhists and Jains; a small shrine dedicated to Thimmamma stands beneath it, childless couples pray here for a child, and a large jatara is held on Shivaratri, drawing thousands. The tree was brought to the world's attention by Bangalore journalist Sathyanarayana (Regret) Iyer, who campaigned for its Guinness record. Note: Kadiri area now falls in Sri Sathya Sai district (carved out of Anantapur in 2022); older sources list Anantapur district. CORRECTION: the CSV town 'Anantapur' is the district; actual location is Gutibayalu village near Kadiri.

name: Thimmamma Marrimanu
town_description: Gutibayalu is a village about 25 km from Kadiri in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh. Its giant banyan tree, Thimmamma Marrimanu, is the area's main attraction, drawing pilgrims and tourists; basic amenities have been developed around the site.
tradition: Folk Hindu worship (revered by Hindus, Buddhists and Jains; small shrine to Thimmamma beneath the tree)

travel.road: About 25 km from Kadiri town by road; roughly 70 km from Horsley Hills (per an APPSC study note).
